newsitem.title: UK: Rates should rise, Bank of England head says.
newsitem.headline: Rates should rise, Bank of England head says.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Monday renewed his call for a "modest pre-emptive" increase in interest rates to prevent a resurgence in inflation.

In a speech prepared for delivery to bankers in Edinburgh, he also said there could be real dangers in allowing justified concern about the damaging effect of the strong pound on exports to deflect attention from the need to tighten monetary policy.
George said it was reasonably certain that strong growth in money supply and consumer spending "cannot be sustained for long consistently with the government's inflation target in the medium term."
The more rapid tightening in the labour market and the recovery in the housing market were further signs that demand might be strengthening.
"That, essentially, is why the Bank has been arguing that we will need at some early stage a modest pre-emptive tightening of monetary policy," George said.

There was no immediate sign of cost or price inflation at the early stages of the production-distribution chain and labour market tightening had not yet resulted in an acceleration of pay settlements.

"But these are backward looking data. If we are to maintain that happy position, we need to anticipate what is to come and begin to moderate the pace of the upswing before the evidence of imbalance comes through into the statistics."
"Two years ago, my message to you was that we needed a stitch in time to save nine, which indeed we did. I bring you the same message again this evening."

George said the position was complicated on this occasion by the recent strength of sterling, which was begiinning to affect export orders. This created a tension between the domestic and external dictates of policy.
"The trouble in this instance is that the stronger exchange rate does not directly affect the build-up of domestic demand pressure, which is the problem we start with," he added.

"It will, if it persists, have a one-off downwards effect (directly or indirectly) on the prices of perhaps a quarter of all goods covered by the retail price index, which will reduce the RPI during the course of this year; but this effect will gradually drop out of the 12-month calculation during 1998."

He said the stronger exchange rate, if it persisted, could cause the external trade balance to weaken and thereby ease pressure on overall demand, but there was a great deal of uncertainty over the timing and scale of these effects.
George said that when a similar dilemma was faced in the 1980s, the domestic expansion was allowed for some time to continue unchecked.
"But in the end we were driven to bring it to a jarring halt," he said.
"I do not suggest for a moment that we are anywhere close to that situation now. Our aim is precisely to avoid that.

"But that experience does illustrate that, in the final analysis, there could be real dangers in allowing justified concern about the exchange rate to deflect us for too long from moving gradually to moderate the upswing," George said. choice ultimately in this situation is not whether or not; it is sooner or later, less or more."

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke left official interest rates unchanged at 6.0 percent at his last monetary meeting with George on January 15, saying the strength of sterling had been a key factor in his decision.

George's remarkably forthright comments suggested he may have advised an interest rate rise at that meeting and been over-ruled, and was likely to press again for a tightening of policy at the next monetary meeting on February 5.
Minutes of the January 15 meeting will be published in six weeks' time.
George said the present dilemma served to illuminate the debate about the economic pros and cons of a single European currency.
On the one hand, the real attractions of fixed exchange rates, especially to manufacturers, were amply apparent.

"On the other hand, our dilemma -- and we are not alone in this dilemma within Europe -- points up the problem that would arise if the single European monetary policy -- the single interest rate -- does not meet the domestic monetary policy needs of all the euro-member countries," George said.

He said he would like to think that European political leaders appreciated the crucial importance of sustainable convergence to the success of monetary union and did not just see it as a technical obstacle to their wider aspirations.
-- Richard Murphy, London Newsroom 44 171 542 7947
